name: Chronic Lymphocytic Inflammation with Pontine Perivascular Enhancement Responsive to Steroids (CLIPPERS)

clinicalPearls: A chronic inflammatory central nervous system disorder centred on the pons and hindbrain, defined by a characteristic imaging pattern and dramatic responsiveness to corticosteroids.
Presents subacutely with brainstem and cerebellar signs: gait ataxia, dysarthria, diplopia, facial or limb paraesthesiae, and internuclear or other ophthalmoplegia.
Hallmark MRI shows myriad small punctate and curvilinear gadolinium-enhancing lesions peppering the pons and adjacent structures, classically likened to 'salt and pepper'.
Enhancing lesions favour the pons but may extend to the middle cerebellar peduncles, medulla, midbrain, cerebellum, spinal cord and occasionally the supratentorial white matter and basal ganglia.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion; lymphoma, glioma, neurosarcoidosis, vasculitis and infection must be rigorously ruled out, ideally with biopsy before or soon after starting steroids.
Histology reveals a dense perivascular and parenchymal T-cell predominant lymphocytic infiltrate without necrosis, granulomas, vessel-wall destruction or a clonal population.
Symptoms and enhancement respond rapidly and completely to corticosteroids, but relapse is typical on tapering, so long-term steroid-sparing immunosuppression is usually required.
Untreated or repeatedly relapsing disease leads to pontine and cerebellar atrophy with fixed disability, underlining the need for sustained immunosuppression.
reference.pathophysiology: CLIPPERS is an idiopathic, presumed autoimmune, inflammatory disorder of the central nervous system with a striking topographical predilection for the pons and surrounding hindbrain structures. The underlying process is a lymphocytic angiocentric inflammation: histopathology demonstrates a dense perivascular cuffing and diffuse parenchymal infiltration by T lymphocytes, predominantly CD4-positive, admixed with variable histiocytes, plasma cells and occasional eosinophils, tracking along small penetrating vessels. Crucially, there is no vessel-wall necrosis or fibrinoid change to indicate a true vasculitis, no well-formed granulomas to suggest sarcoidosis, and no atypical or clonal lymphoid population to indicate lymphoma. The inflammation disrupts the blood-brain barrier, producing the characteristic punctate and linear perivascular contrast enhancement seen on imaging, and the accompanying oedema and demyelination account for the clinical brainstem and cerebellar dysfunction. The consistent responsiveness to corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants supports an immune-mediated mechanism, although no single autoantigen or trigger has been identified; the condition is best regarded as a clinicoradiological-pathological syndrome rather than a single defined disease, and some cases initially labelled CLIPPERS later declare themselves as lymphoma, emphasising its status as a provisional diagnosis requiring ongoing vigilance.
additionalDifferentials: Primary central nervous system lymphoma or lymphomatoid granulomatosis
Primary angiitis of the central nervous system or systemic vasculitis
Brainstem glioma or other infiltrative neoplasm
Demyelinating disease including multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain and spinal cord MRI demonstrating the punctate peppering enhancement pattern and monitoring response
Brain biopsy of an involved region to confirm perivascular T-cell infiltrate and exclude lymphoma and other mimics
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis including cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, cytology and flow cytometry
Serum and CSF autoimmune and vasculitis screen with inflammatory markers and angiotensin-converting enzyme
Whole-body imaging and serum lactate dehydrogenase to screen for occult systemic lymphoma or sarcoidosis
Aquaporin-4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody testing to exclude demyelinating mimics
Serial imaging and clinical review to detect relapse or emergent malignancy
redFlags: Mass-like or ring-enhancing lesions, or enhancement that persists or grows despite steroids, suggesting lymphoma
Progressive brainstem signs with respiratory compromise or reduced consciousness
Systemic features such as weight loss, night sweats or lymphadenopathy pointing to malignancy or sarcoidosis
Rapid clinical deterioration during steroid taper
Atypical cells or clonality on cerebrospinal fluid or tissue analysis
reference.prognosis: With prompt corticosteroids and maintenance immunosuppression the prognosis is generally favourable, with substantial recovery and control of relapses. Delayed treatment or recurrent relapses produce progressive pontine and cerebellar atrophy with permanent neurological disability.
pitfalls: Accepting CLIPPERS without biopsy and thereby missing an underlying lymphoma that transiently responds to steroids
Stopping corticosteroids too quickly, precipitating relapse and cumulative brainstem injury
Mistaking the enhancement pattern for multiple sclerosis or infection and giving inappropriate therapy
Failing to introduce a steroid-sparing agent, leaving patients on long-term high-dose steroids
Overlooking evolution into malignancy on follow-up because of an anchoring diagnosis
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology (standard reference)
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice (standard reference)
Consensus diagnostic criteria for CLIPPERS (standard reference)
management: Induction of remission with high-dose corticosteroids, to which the disorder is characteristically and rapidly responsive.
Steroid-sparing maintenance immunosuppression such as methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil or rituximab to prevent relapse as steroids are withdrawn.
A slow corticosteroid taper, since relapse on rapid withdrawal is characteristic.
Brain biopsy of an involved region before or soon after starting steroids to confirm the perivascular T-cell infiltrate and exclude lymphoma and other mimics.
Serial contrast-enhanced MRI to monitor treatment response, detect relapse and remain vigilant for evolving lymphoma.
Neurorehabilitation for residual ataxia, dysarthria and other brainstem or cerebellar deficits.
Specialist neurology or neuroimmunology follow-up given the risk of progressive pontine and cerebellar atrophy with under-treatment.
